verse.text: For by thee I have run through a troop; and by my God have I leaped over a wall.
verse.summary: David wrote this song on the day the LORD delivered him from all his enemies and from the hand of Saul — a man looking back over years of caves, burned cities and close calls. Notice where he puts the credit: "by thee" and "by my God." The troop was real and the wall was high, but neither had the final word once God was in the fight. Whatever is standing in front of you today, you don't have to break through it in your own strength — run with Him, and watch what you leap over.

sermon.title: Pursue, Overtake, Recover All
sermon.excerpt: Ziklag was ashes, the families were gone, and his own men picked up stones. David didn't start with a counterattack — he encouraged himself in the LORD, asked first, and heard heaven say: pursue, and without fail recover all.

bibleStudy.title: Is It Well?

verses.text: And he said, What then is to be done for her? And Gehazi answered, Verily she hath no child, and her husband is old. And he said, Call her. And when he had called her, she stood in the door. And he said, About this season, according to the time of life, thou shalt embrace a son. And she said, Nay, my lord, thou man of God, do not lie unto thine handmaid. And the woman conceived, and bare a son at that season that Elisha had said unto her, according to the time of life.

So she went and came unto the man of God to mount Carmel. And it came to pass, when the man of God saw her afar off, that he said to Gehazi his servant, Behold, yonder is that Shunammite: Run now, I pray thee, to meet her, and say unto her, Is it well with thee? is it well with thy husband? is it well with the child? And she answered, It is well. And when she came to the man of God to the hill, she caught him by the feet: but Gehazi came near to thrust her away. And the man of God said, Let her alone; for her soul is vexed within her: and the LORD hath hid it from me, and hath not told me. Then she said, Did I desire a son of my lord? did I not say, Do not deceive me?
Women received their dead raised to life again: and others were tortured, not accepting deliverance; that they might obtain a better resurrection:

bibleStudy.excerpt: She told the servant 'It is well' with her dead son on the prophet's bed behind her — not because she was lying, but because she'd already decided exactly who was getting the whole truth.
body: Start with the kind of story Scripture almost never gives space to — not a battle, not a plague, not a king falling off his throne, just a woman in Shunem who notices a traveling preacher passing through her town on a regular circuit and decides, on her own initiative, to do something about it. Twice in two verses the text calls her "a great woman," and before you picture a towering figure in flowing robes, know that the Hebrew is closer to "a woman of substance" — she had land, she had means, she had a household that ran without her having to beg anyone for anything. And what does a woman of substance do with all of that? She builds a room. Not a monument, not a donation with her name engraved on a plaque in the synagogue lobby — a little chamber on the wall, furnished with nothing more than a bed, a table, a stool, and a candlestick, for a prophet who never asked her for a thing. She saw a need nobody told her was there, and she met it before it became an emergency. That is the whole definition of discernment, and most of us never get the credit for the crises we quietly prevent.

Elisha notices, because Elisha always notices, and he does what powerful people rarely do when someone has served them well for free — he asks what he can do back. Through Gehazi he offers her access: a word to the king, a word to the general, real currency in a world where connections were everything. And she turns it down flat. "I dwell among mine own people." Translation: I'm not angling for anything, I don't need a favor cashed in, I built you a room because you needed one, not because I was investing in you. I want you to sit with how rare that is, because most generosity in this life comes with a hidden invoice attached, due the moment the giver needs something back. Hers didn't. Which is exactly why what happens next lands as pure gift and not as payback for services rendered — because she never asked for a son. Gehazi is the one who brings it up: "she hath no child, and her husband is old." She didn't put that need on the table. God noticed what she never mentioned.

So Elisha makes her a promise she never requested: "about this season, according to the time of life, thou shalt embrace a son." And here's where this woman stops being a flannel-graph saint and becomes somebody you actually recognize — she doesn't fall down in grateful tears. She pushes back. "Nay, my lord, thou man of God, do not lie unto thine handmaid." That is not unbelief. That is a woman who has made peace with a closed door and is not interested in having it cracked open just far enough to slam shut again later. Barrenness in that world was a daily, public grief, and she had clearly stopped bidding for a miracle years earlier, for her own protection. If you have ever flinched at a promise because the last one cost you more than it gave back, you are standing exactly where she stood. God didn't rebuke her caution. He simply did it anyway, on schedule, exactly as spoken, and let the boy's own existence answer the argument.

Now here's the part preachers like to rush past on the way to the miracle, and I refuse to rush past it, because the pain is the point. The boy grows. He's old enough to walk out to his father in the harvest field — a normal, ordinary, nothing-is-wrong kind of morning. And then, with no warning the text bothers to explain, he grabs his head and says the only two words anyone remembers him saying in the whole chapter: "My head, my head." A servant carries him to his mother. He sits on her knees. By noon, he is dead. I want you to feel the whiplash of that paragraph the way she felt it in real time — the promise she'd been afraid to trust, fulfilled exactly as spoken, and then, years later, apparently cancelled in a single morning for no stated reason at all. If you have ever received the thing you prayed for and then watched it get ripped back out of your hands before you understood why, you are not reading a story that happened to someone else. You are reading your own Tuesday with different names attached.

Watch what she does, because this is where the sermon actually starts. She doesn't scream. She doesn't summon the neighbors. She carries her dead son up the stairs, lays him on the very bed she built for the prophet with her own hands years earlier — the chamber she furnished before she ever needed anything from the man who'd sleep in it — shuts the door, and goes to get a donkey. When her husband, confused, asks why she's suddenly riding out on a random weekday, she gives him four words that could mean anything: "It shall be well." Then she tells the servant driving the donkey, "slack not thy riding for me, except I bid thee" — in other words, do not slow down for my comfort, I didn't come out here to take it easy. That is a woman managing a catastrophe with both hands while telling absolutely no one the full truth of what's happening, because she has already decided exactly one person is getting the whole story, and it isn't her husband and it isn't the help.

Elisha spots her coming from a distance and sends Gehazi ahead with the obvious question: "Is it well with thee? is it well with thy husband? is it well with the child?" And she gives him the same four words again — "It is well." Now, don't you dare read that as a lie, and don't you dare read it as denial either, because those are not the same thing and this story is the clearest place in all of Scripture to learn the difference. Denial is pretending the body isn't on the bed. She knows exactly what's on the bed. This is something else — a woman who has decided that Gehazi, a servant with no authority to fix anything, is not the person this particular truth belongs to. She is not managing her image. She is managing her access. Some of you have been bleeding out in front of people who could offer you sympathy but could never offer you a solution, and you've worn yourself out trying to make them understand the depth of it. She skips that entirely. "It is well" is not what she tells people who can't help. It's what she says on her way to the one who can.

And then she reaches Elisha, and everything changes. She falls at his feet — not a polite greeting, a full collapse — and when Gehazi moves to push her off, the prophet stops him cold: "Let her alone; for her soul is vexed within her." And here, finally, in front of the one man in the story who can actually do something about it, the composed woman disappears and the furious, grieving mother says exactly what's been sitting in her chest the whole ride: "Did I desire a son of my lord? did I not say, Do not deceive me?" That is not a woman thanking God for a miracle. That is a woman all but accusing the prophet of setting her up — I told you not to get my hopes up, and you did it anyway, and now look. Here's my real question for you today: who is your Gehazi, and who is your Elisha? Because you need both answers ready — the composed "it is well" for the people who were never going to be able to fix it anyway, and the raw, unfiltered, borderline-accusatory honesty you owe to the only One who actually can. God can handle your "did I desire this" far better than He can handle you performing peace in front of Him that you don't actually have.

So Elisha goes up, shuts the door — just the two of them and the body, no audience, no spectacle — and stretches himself out over the child, once, and the flesh is still cold. He gets up, walks the house, and does it again. This time the boy sneezes seven times and opens his eyes. Not a slow recovery. Not a fever breaking. A dead child, alive, in the same room where his mother once laid a bed, a table, a stool, and a candlestick for a man she didn't know would one day need that room to do exactly this. The writer of Hebrews, centuries later, reaches all the way back into stories like this one and writes, without naming her, "women received their dead raised to life again." She never gets a name in that verse. She barely gets one in her own chapter — "that Shunammite" is as specific as it gets. And yet she is permanently enshrined in the New Testament's own hall of faith, uncredited, unnamed, and absolutely included.

So carry both halves of her out of this chapter, because you'll need both before the year is over. There will be people in your life who only deserve the composed answer — "it is well" — not because you're lying to them, but because the full weight of what you're carrying was never theirs to hold, and handing it to them wouldn't move you one inch closer to your miracle. And there will be exactly one door you need to walk through, fall down in front of, and tell the unfiltered truth — did I desire this, did I not say don't deceive me, here is exactly how vexed my soul actually is. God is not asking you to perform peace for Him. He already knows what's on the bed. He's simply waiting for you to stop managing your image with Him and start managing your access to Him instead. Go find your mountain. Go find the One who can actually raise what's dead in your life. And when you get there, tell Him everything. In Jesus' name, amen.

lines: Father, I declare today that I will not sit in the ashes of what the enemy burned — I encourage myself in the LORD my God!
My tears have had their night, but they do not get the final word over my life!
Every stone of blame and accusation lifted against me falls to the ground, in the name of Jesus!
I enquire of the LORD before I move — and when He says pursue, I pursue!
By my God I run through a troop, and by my God I leap over every wall in my way!
I shall surely overtake, and without fail I shall recover all!
I take back my peace, my joy, my health and my finances — nothing lacking, neither small nor great!
I take back my children, my marriage and my fire for God — the enemy was only holding what belongs to me!
The LORD restores the years the locust has eaten, and my Ziklag becomes the doorway to my crowning!
Save this. Speak it over your house today. I pursue, I overtake, and I recover all! In Jesus' mighty name, amen!

dreamFire.title: A Wall of Fire Round About Me
dreamFire.intro: Tonight's shield prayer is not a guess at your dream — it is Zechariah's promise sent ahead of you into the dark: a wall of fire no power can climb, tunnel under, or see through. Pray it out loud and let the fire stand before you sleep.
points: Father, by the authority of Zechariah 2:5, I decree a wall of fire round about me tonight — before my body, behind my back, over my bed, and around every border of my sleep — no power shall cross it, in the mighty name of Jesus!
Every evil altar lit on the far side of my wall of fire tonight, burn down to ash before the hand that struck the match can finish its rites, in the name of Jesus!

Any power that runs to chase me, waits to trap me, or schemes to trade my portion for another's in the dream realm tonight meets my wall of fire first and is turned back scorched, in Jesus' mighty name!
Every mark, ring, garment, or covering any hand attempts to throw over my wall of fire tonight catches flame in the air and falls to ash before it ever reaches my skin, in the name of Jesus!

Every witchcraft table set to study me, call my name, or cast a vote over my life tonight loses my scent and my shadow the moment my wall of fire rises — you are searching for someone you cannot find, in Jesus' mighty name!
Every pit dug for me in the dream realm tonight, by the word of the Lord, swallows its own digger before the sun comes up, in the name of Jesus!
Every rope, net, or chain thrown across my wall of fire tonight burns through before it ever tightens — I was not born to be bound, and I will not be bound in my sleep, in Jesus' mighty name!

Every gate assigned to work against me between midnight and daybreak — gate of delay, gate of sickness, gate of confusion, gate of loss — stands outside my wall of fire and shall not open, in the mighty name of Jesus!

If my spirit has been summoned, detained, or carried anywhere outside my wall of fire tonight, I sound the trumpet of recall now — spirit, soul, and body, come home whole and untouched, in Jesus' mighty name!

Let my wall of fire stretch over my household tonight — every room, every bed, every name under this roof covered — so that no darkness assigned against this house gets past the flame, in the name of Jesus!

Every evil court convened outside my wall tonight to pass a verdict on my life, your judgment cannot cross the fire and cannot find me — I stand inside a better court, and the Judge of that court is my Father, in Jesus' mighty name!

So I decree over tonight: the wall is fire, the fire is the blood, and the blood has already spoken — no weapon formed in the dark shall prosper, no power gathered against me shall find a way in, and I will rise in the morning exactly as I lay down: covered, untouched, and victorious, in the mighty, all-consuming name of Jesus Christ, amen! 🔥
